assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength lattice proposal and Ye's demonstration of extreme coherence and systematic control, take atomic frequency measurement to the 1e-18 level and beyond. This is measurement science of the kind that defines what we can know, with direct consequences for redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. From an atomic-physics perspective the originality (state-insensitive trapping of neutral atoms) and the clarity of the achievement are very high.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first realisations with Sr; Ye brought the clock to record accuracy and coherence and developed the many-body and systematics understanding. The two-name credit is a clean prize configuration. Other contributors (e.g. Lemonde, Ludlow, and the Sr/Yb community) are not in the supplied credit, and Ye's partly overlapping role in other candidates should not influence this one.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently in many laboratories with Sr, Yb and other species, with international clock comparisons and ongoing work toward redefining the second. Interpretation is stable, the technique is mature, and recognition is timely, arguably overdue given that Hall and Hansch (frequency combs, 2005) and Wineland (ion clocks, 2012) laid parts of the ground.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier Nobel recognition of frequency combs and ion-based optical clocks may be argued as incremental by some members.
The practical redefinition of the second has not yet been formally adopted, so societal impact is still prospective.
I do not independently verify the detailed priority chronology between lattice-clock proposals.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation with ions turned quantum information processing into an experimental discipline; trapped-ion systems remain among the most coherent and best controlled quantum platforms. Originality and lasting impact are high, and the link to laser cooling, spectroscopy and coherent light-matter control is close to my own field.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the theoretical proposal; Blatt led the early and sustained experimental demonstrations of gates, entanglement and quantum simulation. Wineland and Haroche were recognised in 2012 for control of individual quantum systems, which overlaps in part; Wineland and colleagues (e.g. at NIST) also made decisive gate demonstrations, but the supplied credit does not include them, so the three-name configuration is chosen from the supplied names. The theory-plus-experiment pairing is natural.
assessment.maturity: Thirty years of replicated work in many groups, with commercial scale-up of ion-trap machines. Recognition is mature, though part of the field was already honoured in 2012, which weakens novelty of the prize as a whole.
uncertainties: Degree of overlap with the 2012 prize and whether Wineland-group gate contributions need separate recognition.
Zoller and Cirac also appear in the optical-lattice candidate, so the committee may prefer to spread them across a single prize.
The scalability of trapped-ion computing remains an open question, but this does not affect the discovery itself.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses laser-manipulated matter waves for exquisitely sensitive measurements of gravity, rotation, the fine-structure constant and tests of the equivalence principle. It extends the Chu, Cohen-Tannoudji and Phillips line of laser-cooling work and is, to my mind, a prime example of measurement precision driving new physics. Importance, originality and clarity are strong.
assessment.attribution: Bordé developed the theory and early light-pulse concepts, Pritchard demonstrated the first atom interferometers and pioneered the matter-wave approach with Ketterle-era collaborators, and Kasevich (with Chu) realised precision light-pulse gravimetry and gyroscopes. Chu was already recognised in 1997 and other pioneers (e.g. Keith, Mlynek, Chu, Rasel) are not in the supplied credit; the three-name configuration is plausible but the priority among early demonstrations is not trivially settled.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across many laboratories and field-deployable instruments exist; fundamental-physics applications (gravitational-wave detection proposals, equivalence-principle tests) are still developing, so some of the impact is prospective.
uncertainties: Contested priority in the early 1990s between several groups.
Overlap with the 1997 laser-cooling prize.
The big fundamental-physics payoffs have not yet been realised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type Hamiltonians with tunable parameters, giving quantum simulation of many-body phases, the superfluid-Mott transition, and now single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. The importance is high and the technique is rooted in laser cooling and trapping, with consequences across condensed-matter and quantum-information physics.
assessment.attribution: The proposal side (Jaksch, Zoller, Cirac) and the experimental side (Greiner and Bloch for the Mott transition and microscopy, Esslinger for fermionic Hubbard physics) are both essential. With five credited names, the prize configuration must pick three; I choose the experimental trio, accepting that omitting Zoller and Cirac leaves the theory contribution unrecognised here, though they are covered in the trapped-ion candidate.
assessment.maturity: A broadly confirmed experimental field with many independent groups and increasingly quantitative simulations; the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize cover related ground. Quantum advantage over classical simulation has begun to be argued but is not settled.
uncertainties: Allocation among five credited people is difficult and any three-person selection is partial.
Whether the quantum-simulation payoff is already demonstrated beyond classical methods remains debated.
Overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical addressing and readout of single spins in diamond and other solid-state defects, together with nanoscale quantum sensing, have produced room-temperature quantum sensors for magnetic fields, temperature and electric fields at the nanoscale. This closely fits the idea that progress is limited by what we can measure and how accurately, and spans spectroscopy, quantum optics and biological sensing. The originality of single-defect optical spin detection and its sensing applications is high.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated optically detected magnetic resonance of single NV centres, Awschalom developed coherent control of defect spins in several materials, and Walsworth with Lukin and others developed nanoscale magnetometry and diamond sensing. Lukin is in the credited names and is equally strong; I keep three names but the allocation between Lukin and Walsworth is a real ambiguity. Gruber, Jelezko and Maze/Hanson-type contributions are also relevant but are not in the credit.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups replicate the effect and commercial quantum-sensing products exist, but several flagship applications (single-molecule NMR, in vivo sensing) remain developing; the field is mature enough in its core but still moving.
uncertainties: Allocation among four names, notably Lukin versus Walsworth, is unresolved.
Missing credit for other early NV pioneers such as Jelezko.
Some of the applications are still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics transplants cavity QED to superconducting circuits and underlies today's leading superconducting quantum processors, strong coupling, dispersive readout and quantum-limited amplification. The impact is very high and the concept is clear and original.
assessment.attribution: Blais and Wallraff, with Schoelkopf and collaborators, established the architecture and its first strong-coupling demonstration; the supplied names fit a natural set. I note that part of the superconducting-circuit field was recognised by the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which overlaps in subject but not in the discovery.
assessment.maturity: Extremely well confirmed and industrially adopted, though quantum computing itself remains an evolving technology; timing is good but the recent circuit-related prize makes immediate recognition less likely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the recent prize on superconducting circuits.
Contributions of other groups, notably the Devoret and Martinis circle, are not in the credited names.
Whether the architecture or the broader processor effort is the prize-worthy unit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, followed by the experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, opened a new class of quantum matter. Importance and originality are high, although the field lies outside my own expertise and I defer to colleagues on condensed-matter detail.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the Z2 classification and the graphene-based prediction; Molenkamp led the HgTe experiment following Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's proposal, and Hasan led early 3D topological insulator observations. The supplied credit does not include Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu or Konig, so the three-name configuration is a compromise and Hasan's claim is real.
assessment.maturity: Widely confirmed across many materials and platforms; recognition is timely, though the Haldane/Thouless/Kosterlitz prize of 2016 covers related topology and may be seen as overlapping.
uncertainties: Excluding Hasan and the BHZ proposal leaves allocation of credit disputed.
Overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize.
My limited expertise in this subfield.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays give a platform with optically trapped atoms, strongly interacting through Rydberg states, for quantum simulation and gates. The concept ties closely to laser spectroscopy and coherent atom-light control and has progressed rapidly with demonstrated many-body simulation and error-corrected logical-qubit experiments.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and collaborators proposed Rydberg gates, Saffman and others developed the gate scheme, Browaeys demonstrated blockade between individual atoms and Lukin led programmable arrays; Zoller is credited but also appears elsewhere, and I select three of the four credited names knowing the theory credit is partly sacrificed.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly developing; the key experiments are confirmed by several groups, but the field is young enough that the lasting component may not yet be settled and recognition could be premature.
uncertainties: Possible prematurity given the pace of ongoing development.
Choice of three out of four credited names is contestable.
Distinct contributions of blockade versus tweezer arrays may need separate treatment.
